1570	## 13. CLI reference
1571	
1572	Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
1573	✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
1574	and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
1575	coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
1576	text and stdout carries the bare results.
1577	
1578	| Command | Behaviour |
1579	| --- | --- |
1580	| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
1581	| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
1582	| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
1583	| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
1584	| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1585	| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
1586	| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
1587	| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1588	| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
1589	| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
1590	| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
1591	| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
1592	| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
1593	| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |

1600	
1601	`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:
1602

1604	  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled

1611	  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,

1614	  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in

1616	  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
1617	- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
1618	  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and

1665	## 15. Working on a specbase
1666	
1667	1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
1668	   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
1669	   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
1670	   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
1671	   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
1672	   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
1673	2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
1674	   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
1675	   follow them only when relevant.
1676	3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
1677	   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
1678	   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
1679	   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
1680	     `lib/` folder;
1681	   - lowerCamelCase property names;
1682	   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
1683	   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
1684	   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
1685	   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
1686	4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
1687	   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
1688	   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
1689	5. **Validate.**
1690	   - Run `piton check`.
1691	   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
1692	     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
1693	     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
1694	     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
1695	   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
1696	   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
1697	   - Run `piton format --check`.
1698	6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
1699	   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
1700	   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
1701	   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
1702	7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
1703	   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
1704	   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
1705	   flag the gap.
1706	
1707	## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec
1708	
1709	Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:
1710	
1711	- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
1712	  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
1713	  `format` with no path or `-`.
1714	
1715	- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
1716	  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
1717	  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.
1718	
1719	Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
1720	surprise you:
1721	
1722	- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
1723	  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
1724	  package.
1725	- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
1726	  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
1727	  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
1728	  the value on the anchor itself.
1729	- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
1730	  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
1731	- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
1732	  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
1733	  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
1734	- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
1735	  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
1736	- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
1737	  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
1738	  adapter `.pi` files.
1739	# Planning
1740	
1741	## How To Build
1742	
1743	A Planning should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A Planning should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.
1744	
1745	## Theme
1746	
1747	Drawn in the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.
1748	
1749	## Pitch
1750	
1751	A plain, quick list of the work still to do, as Linear keeps issues: stories written ahead of time, each saying how it will be sent, Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, or Freeform, gathered into the next sprint and sent to the agent in order, all at once.
1752	
1753	## Description
1754	
1755	Planning opens in a tab of its own in the body, "Planning", with a checklist icon, as a file opens, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) says, from the ribbon's Planning tab or the palette's "Planning". It is one column of stories, at most 760 pixels wide, centred, in sections, each headed by its name and count: "Current sprint", at the top, only while a sprint is under way, then "Next sprint", and "Backlog" beneath them. A section with nothing in it reads, muted, "Nothing planned" or "Backlog is empty".
1756	
1757	## Stories
1758	
1759	A story is one piece of work, written as it will be sent: a title, a prompt, and how it will be sent. Each is a row, 36 pixels tall: a drag grip at its left; a small mode picker, a pill reading its mode, "Code", "Chain", "Spec", "Ask", or "Freeform", in that mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it; its title, in the body's text colour, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, muted, a small icon for anything attached, and, once it has been sent, its status as a task's is shown. Hovering a row shows a menu button at its right. A story has no Send of its own, as the sprint says.
1760	Clicking a row opens it beneath, expanded in place, the others moving down: its title, editable in place; its prompt, in a [GrowingTextInput](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input) with the chat input's highlighting, completions, and slicing, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) has, and its attachments beneath; and its parameters, its mode, model, effort, and Slice, as the chat input shows them. Every change is saved as it is made. Only one story is open at a time; Escape or clicking its row again closes it.
1761	
1762	## Creating
1763	
1764	Creating a story is quick. A "New story" line at the foot of Next sprint, and Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS) while Planning has focus, adds a story at the end of Next sprint, open, its title focused, in the mode last picked for a story. However a story is added, it goes into Next sprint, at its end: a new story, a duplicate, and one added from an Ask answer's card with "Add to sprint" alike. It can then be moved to the Backlog to wait, as the sprint says. The one exception is an accepted proposal for a new story, from drafting, research, or an Ask answer's proposal card, which goes into the Backlog, at its end, as the proposal cards say, and reaches a sprint only once it is moved to Next sprint. Typing a title and pressing Enter adds it and starts another beneath it, so a list can be written down without the mouse; Escape on an empty one removes it. A title with no prompt sends its title as its prompt.
1765	A story can also be prompted into existence: "Draft stories", a button beside the Backlog's heading, opens a small box to say what is wanted, in a sentence or a paragraph, and asks the harness, in a run of its own with no session, with the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts), to break it into stories, each with a title, a prompt, and the mode that fits it. They come back as proposals, as the drafting and proposals say, each to be accepted, edited, or rejected, and none reaches the plan until it is accepted. An Ask answer's prompt cards also offer "Add to sprint", which adds the card's prompt as a story in its mode to Next sprint.
1766	
1767	## Sprint
1768	
1769	Stories move between the Backlog and Next sprint by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, across the sections as within them, or from a row's menu, "Move to next sprint" or "Move to backlog". Their order within Next sprint is the order they will be sent. A row's menu also has "Duplicate" and "Delete".
1770	"Send sprint", a primary button at the right of Next sprint's heading, enabled while it holds a story, sends every story in it, in order, as though each had been written in the chat input on its mode's tab and sent, one after another, as the [PromptSending](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says: each task queues in its lane behind the one before it, in the order of the sprint, and each question runs at once. The stories go into the queue as one block, so nothing sent later comes between them, and the queue's auto-send carries them on as ever, as the [QueueList](../prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list) says.
1771	Each story starts a conversation of its own, as though New conversation had been pressed just before it, and so does each later step of a story's chain: a story never carries on the conversation of the story before it, nor of anything its lane ran before the sprint. New conversation, pressed before the sprint was sent, is left for the next prompt written in the chat input.
1772	A story can't be sent on its own. The only way a story reaches work is through the sprint: a story in the Backlog waits until it is moved into Next sprint and the sprint is sent, and a story in Next sprint goes when the sprint does. Nothing in Planning, its rows, their menus, the open story, the keyboard, the palette, or the ribbon, sends a single story, and nothing elsewhere sends a story by any other route: a story can't be dragged or copied into the chat input or the queue to be sent from there, and its menu has no "Send" or "Edit in chat input". The chat input's own prompts are not stories and are sent as ever; once a prompt is a story, the sprint is its only way to work. To send one story at once, it is the only story in Next sprint when Send sprint is pressed. A story that failed or was cancelled is sent again the same way, with the next sprint.
1773	Sending the sprint moves its stories into a "Current sprint" section, above Next sprint, shown only while it holds a story, so Next sprint is empty again and stories added meanwhile go there, to be the sprint after. A story in Current sprint keeps its place, its row showing its task's status as it queues, runs, and ends, and clicking it opens its task in the Tasks tab; it can't be moved or edited there. Once every story of Current sprint has ended, the section offers "Close sprint", which moves the stories that are done into a muted, collapsed "Done" list beneath the Backlog, and those that failed, were cancelled, or stopped to the start of Next sprint, in their order, to be sent again. While a sprint is current, Send sprint is disabled, its tooltip saying a sprint is already under way.
1774	Send sprint only ever moves into Current sprint the stories it actually sent. A story with nothing to send, its title and its prompt both empty, is skipped: it stays in Next sprint, where it was, and Send sprint's result says, muted, how many it skipped and why, as "1 empty story left in Next sprint". A sprint where every story is empty sends nothing and makes no Current sprint.
1775	Once a sprint is done, it can always be closed. Every story of Current sprint counts as ended once its task has ended, done, failed, cancelled, or stopped, or once its task can no longer be found, as when its record was deleted, it was never recorded, or the application quit before it was. A story whose task is missing is never shown as Queued, or as anything still to come: its row reads "Task missing", muted, in the theme's warning colour, its tooltip saying its task can't be found, and it counts as ended and not Done. A story still waiting in its lane's queue, or held for review, as the paused section says, is still to come and hasn't ended. So Close sprint shows as soon as no story of Current sprint is building, compiling, running, paused, queued, or held, and never waits on a task that can't arrive.
1776	Close sprint treats a story whose task is missing as it treats one that failed or was cancelled: it goes back to the start of Next sprint, with the others sent again, in their order, never into Done. Closing saves the sections, Done, Next sprint, the Backlog, and the emptied Current sprint, to `order.json` straight away, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, and Current sprint's state is worked out afresh from the stories' tasks whenever the plan is read, so a sprint that finished, or whose tasks went missing, before a reload or a restart can still be closed after it, as before.
1777	
1778	## Auto Start
1779	
1780	Next sprint can start on its own: a "Start automatically" switch on Next sprint's heading, beside Send sprint, its tooltip saying the next sprint starts as soon as the current one is done. It starts off, and is saved with the plan, in `order.json`, so it is kept across reloads and restarts.
1781	While it is on, once every story of Current sprint has ended Done, the current sprint closes by itself, as Close sprint closes it, and Next sprint, if it holds a story, is sent at once, as Send sprint sends it, with nobody having to start it; and while no sprint is current, a story added to an empty Next sprint starts it the same way. A sprint that ended with a story failed, cancelled, stopped, or with its task missing, never starts the next by itself: it waits, Close sprint offered as ever, and the switch's row says, in the theme's warning colour, why the next didn't start. Nor does the next start while planning is paused, as the paused section says: it starts once the pause is ended by Resume, or Approve, if the switch is still on. An empty Next sprint starts nothing.
1782	Each time a sprint starts by itself, a passive notification says so, "Next sprint started: 4 stories", with a link that opens Planning, and the debug log records it. Turning the switch off never stops a sprint already sent; it only keeps the next from starting by itself. Turning it on while no sprint is current and Next sprint holds a story starts Next sprint at once, as adding a story to it would, unless planning is paused.
1783	The switch works while Planning isn't open, from the plan as saved, whichever tab is shown. When the project is opened, or the application starts, with the switch on, no sprint current, and Next sprint holding a story, it doesn't start by itself; the switch's row says, muted, "Waiting to start", with a "Start now" button, so a sprint never begins unseen as the application opens. A current sprint whose stories were cut off when the application quit, as every run is, ended them, and never starts the next by itself.
1784	While the switch is on, Next sprint's heading shows "Auto" beside its count, in the theme's accent, and the ribbon's Send Sprint button's tooltip says the next sprint starts automatically.
1785	
1786	## Saving
1787	
1788	The stories, their order, and which section each is in are saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, in `.suspense/planning/`, a file per story, holding its hidden anchor as a queued prompt's is, and an `order.json` listing the sections and their stories, so the plan is kept with the project and comes back as it was left. A story's steps are saved in its own file, in their order, as its steps say, never apart from it.
1789	
1790	## Steps
1791	
1792	A story can have steps: one or more further prompts, each a piece of the story done after the one before, as a chain's steps are. Each step has a prompt, a mode of its own, Code or Spec, starting as the story's, and a model and effort, starting as the story's, and may have attachments. A story with no steps is just its own prompt, as before; its prompt is always its first step.
1793	An open story lists its steps beneath its prompt, in order, each a row numbered from 2, the story's own prompt being 1, with its mode pill and the first line of its prompt, opening in place to edit, as a story does. "Add step", beneath the last, adds one at the end, open and focused; several can be added one after another, Enter in an empty step's prompt adding none. Steps are reordered by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, or Alt+Up and Alt+Down, and each has a remove button in its row and in its menu. The story's own prompt stays first and can't be moved among them.
1794	A step belongs to its story and to nothing else. It is saved in the story's file, in a `steps` list of the story's hidden anchor, in its order, and saved as every change to the plan is, straight away; a story duplicated copies its steps, and one deleted deletes them. Its order is kept wherever the story goes, between sections, into a sprint, and back from Done.
1795	Wherever the story is shown, its steps are too: its row in Planning shows how many after its title, muted, as "3 steps", with the list in its tooltip; the open story lists them as above; a proposal to add to it shows them, so what it would add to can be seen; and once it is sent, it is sent as a chain, its prompt first and each step after it in order, each step sent only once the one before it finishes, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s chained tasks are, so the Tasks tab shows the story as one chain with its steps beneath it. A story sent can't be given more steps; its steps, sent or still to come, read as they were sent. In Current sprint, a story with steps is expanded, a row for each step beneath it, in order, indented 16 pixels, each with its own status, as a running chain's are in the Tasks tab; in Done, and in a finding started from the story, its steps are listed the same way, collapsed to its step count until it is expanded. The same steps, in the same order, are what every place shows, since every place reads them from the story's own file.
1796	A step is only ever added to a story that exists. Adding one to a story that doesn't, as one deleted while a proposal naming it waited, or by another window, or whose file was removed from `.suspense/planning/` meanwhile, changes nothing: no story is made for it, no other story is given it, and nothing is saved. It says so in plain words where it was asked for, as "That story no longer exists, so the step wasn't added", in the theme's error colour, as the states say, with what was to be added kept, so it can be added to another story or as a new one. A step added to a story already sent is refused the same way, saying the story has been sent.
1797	
1798	## Layout
1799	
1800	Everything in Planning is laid out on one rhythm, so it scans as a single list. The column has 24 pixels of padding at its top and sides. Each section's heading is a row 32 pixels tall: its name in small semibold text, its count beside it, muted, and its actions at its right, each a labelled button, never an icon alone; 8 pixels beneath it its first row. Story rows are 36 pixels tall, 2 pixels apart, each with 12 pixels of padding at either side, their parts in fixed columns, so the grips, mode pills, titles, and statuses line up down the whole list: the grip 16 pixels, the mode pill 72 pixels, the title the rest, the status and time right-aligned in a column of their own 96 pixels wide, then the row's buttons. Sections are 24 pixels apart. Every row's state reads the same way, as below, and every label is the same small text, muted where it is secondary.
1801	From top to bottom, Planning reads: the pause bar, while paused; Current sprint, while a sprint is under way; Next sprint; Backlog; Findings; and Done, collapsed. Each is a section headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same three parts, below.
1802	
1803	## Parts
1804	
1805	Everything in Planning is built from three parts, each always drawn the same way:
1806	- A row: 36 pixels tall, in the fixed columns above, for stories, steps, findings, and Done; its secondary text muted and cut off with an ellipsis, its buttons small ghost buttons with labels, shown at its right on hover and always while it is focused
1807	- A panel: an inset area 16 pixels below what opened it, on the theme's raised surface, corners rounded 6 pixels, 12 pixels of padding, a heading row of 32 pixels with its name, as "Draft stories", "Research", or the story's title, and its close button, its content beneath, and its actions in a footer row, right-aligned, the primary action last; used for an open story, drafting, and research
1808	- A card: a box inside a panel, on the theme's base surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 4 pixels, 12 pixels of padding, 8 pixels from the next; a label row at its top, its content, and a footer row of labelled buttons; used for proposals and for each finding's summary
1809	Labels are words, never icons alone: every button reads what it does, "Accept", "Send sprint", "Start automatically", and an icon beside a label only repeats it. Each heading's count is a plain number, muted, and each status a coloured label, as the states say. The pause bar is a row across the column's top, 40 pixels tall, its text and buttons on one line, the same height whatever it says.
1810	
1811	## States
1812	
1813	Each part of Planning has the same few states, shown the same way wherever they come up, so a state is never guessed from what is missing.
1814	- Empty: a single muted line, centred in the section, saying what is missing and what to do, as "Nothing planned. Drag stories here, or press Ctrl+N.", with no illustration
1815	- Loading: a spinner and a short muted label of what is happening, as "Drafting stories…", in the place the result will appear, never a blank space
1816	- Paused: a story whose task is paused shows "Paused" as its status, in the theme's warning colour, with a small pause icon, and a "Resume" button in its row, as the PromptSending says of pausing; a sprint with any story paused says so in its heading, as "1 paused", in the same colour
1817	- Error: a line in the theme's error colour, saying what went wrong in plain words, with what the harness or the application reported beneath it collapsed under "Details", and a "Try again" button where trying again can help
1818	A story's status in its row is the same coloured label a task has, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says, Queued, Running with its spinner and time, Done, Failed, Cancelled, Paused, or, where its task can't be found, Task missing, as the sprint says, and a story not yet sent shows nothing there, so its absence means "not sent".
1819	Each part shows each state that can come up for it, worded for it:
1820	- Story list: empty, "Nothing planned. Press Ctrl+N to add a story." in Next sprint and "Nothing waiting." in the Backlog; loading, while the plan is read on opening, a row of skeleton rows, never an empty section; error, when the plan can't be read or saved, saying which file and why, with "Try again"
1821	- Research and its findings: loading, the live line of what it is reading with its spinner; empty, "No findings yet." in Findings; error, the run's failure with "Try again", which keeps the question in its box; a finding that ended early, as stopped, marked "Incomplete", muted, in its row
1822	- Pause: the pause bar, in the theme's warning colour, as the paused section says, and the sprint's Send buttons disabled with their tooltips saying why; a sprint that can't start for a failed story says so in its heading, in the same colour
1823	- Proposals: loading, the drafting line and spinner; empty, "No stories proposed." with "Draft again"; error, the run's failure with "Try again"; a proposal with no spec cited, in the warning colour with "Draft again", as the spec grounding says
1824	
1825	## Drafting
1826	
1827	Drafting stories shows its work in one place, a panel opened beneath the Backlog's heading, never in a popup that hides the list. It has the request box at its top, labelled "Describe what you want", and beneath it, while the run goes, its research: a muted line of what the harness is doing, as "Reading the spec…", with its spinner, updating as it goes, and a "Stop" button. Once it ends, the panel lists its proposals, as below, then "Accept all" and "Reject all" buttons along the panel's foot, and closes itself once none is left to decide. A run that fails shows its error, as the states say, and leaves the request in its box to try again; one that proposes nothing says so, as an empty state. Proposals are kept until each is decided, so closing Planning and coming back finds them as they were.
1828	Drafting can also be started from an open story, with "Ask agent" in its row's menu or the open story's footer: the request box then reads "What does this story need?", the run is told the story's title and prompt, and the panel opens beneath that story rather than the Backlog's heading.
1829	The request is sent with the panel's "Draft" button, its primary action, or by pressing Enter in the request box, whichever label it reads; Ctrl+Enter there starts it too, and the button's tooltip gives Enter as its shortcut. Shift+Enter adds a new line in the box and sends nothing. A request that is empty, or only spaces and new lines, starts nothing, and the button is disabled while it is. While a run is going, Enter starts no second one, and the button is disabled. Enter in the request box only ever sends the request: the list's Enter, opening or closing the focused story, never fires while focus is in the box.
1830	
1831	## Proposals
1832	
1833	The agent never writes the plan itself. Its run is a Question run, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, able to read the project and change nothing, and Suspense data is never granted to it, so it can't touch `.suspense/planning/`; it only proposes, and nothing it proposes reaches the plan until the user accepts it.
1834	Each proposal is one concrete task, with a title, a prompt, and the mode that fits it, and says where it should go: either "New story", to become a story of its own, or "Add to" a story, naming an existing story the run was shown, the open story first, to be added to it. The planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts) asks for each proposal as a fenced block whose info string is `suspense-story`, holding its title, its mode, its target, `new` or the story's id, its `spec` list of citations into the Piton source, as the spec grounding says, and its prompt, so the application reads it whatever else the reply says. The planning prompt explains the form with an example, as:
1835	```suspense-story
1836	title: Close a finished sprint
1837	mode: chain
1838	target: new
1839	spec:
1840	- spec/scope/planning/index.pi#Planning.sprint: when Close sprint shows
1841	- No match: archiving a closed sprint
1842	prompt:
1843	Close sprint is offered once every story of the current sprint has
1844	ended, as spec/scope/planning/index.pi#Planning.sprint says.
1845	```
1846	A block that names a story that no longer exists is shown as "New story", with a muted note saying so.
1847	
1848	## Spec Grounding
1849	
1850	A drafted story is grounded in the project's spec, never written from the request alone. Before proposing, the drafter searches the spec for what each story touches: the requirements and behaviours it changes or relies on, the names it uses, as a feature, a component, or a property, and the sections they are in. It reads the spec as every run does, from its compiled reference or from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, and the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts) tells it to.
1851	Each proposal cites what it found, specifically: its `suspense-story` block holds a `spec` list, one entry per element, each a link to the element in the spec's Piton source, under the spec location, never to the compiled reference: the .pi file, relative to the project directory, then `#` and the element it names, an anchor or a property on one, in the form `piton slice` takes, as `spec/scope/planning/index.pi#Planning.sprint`, with a short line of what in it the story touches. The story's prompt names those elements and links to them in the same form. Only elements the drafter found are cited, and where they point is the only thing that is Piton source: the drafter still learns what the spec says only from the compiled reference or from what `piton slice` prints, never by reading the Piton source, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, and works out each element's source from what `piton slice` prints for it, which names the file each declaration is in.
1852	The application checks each link against the Piton source when the proposal arrives: the file has to exist under the spec location, and has to define the named element, the anchor declared in it and, for a property, that property on it, as `piton slice` would find it. A link that fails either check is dropped, with a muted note on the card saying which link it dropped and why, "no such file" or "the file doesn't define Planning.sprint". Each citation, on the proposal card and in an accepted story's "Spec" list, opens that place in the Piton source, the file in the editor at the element's declaration, as the [OpenFile](../open-file/index.md#open-file) opens a file.
1853	Where no spec element matches part of a story, as a request for something the spec doesn't describe yet, the story says so instead of inventing one: its `spec` list holds an entry reading "No match", with what was looked for, and its prompt says plainly that the spec has nothing on it yet, so the change is new. A proposal with no element at all, and no "No match", isn't shown as a story: its card says the drafter cited no spec, in the theme's warning colour, with "Draft again", which runs the draft for that story once more.
1854	The citations are shown on the proposal's card, beneath its prompt, as a short list, each element's name, as `Planning.sprint`, and its file, muted, as a link that opens that place in the Piton source, a "No match" entry muted with a small marker, and are kept with the story once it is accepted, listed in the open story beneath its steps as "Spec", and shown in its row's tooltip. They can be edited with the story, removed, or added to by hand: "Add citation" opens a picker of the spec's elements, its anchors and their properties, found from the Piton source and searched by name, never from the compiled reference, and adds the one picked in the same form, checked as a proposal's are.
1855	Each citation says what kind of element it is, "Requirement", "Behaviour", "Name", or "Section", shown as a small muted label before it, and quotes the few words of the spec it rests on, so what the story relies on can be checked at a glance. Grounding holds for every proposal, however it came: from Draft stories, from research that ends with proposals, and from an Ask answer's `suspense-story` block, each checked and flagged the same way when it arrives.
1856	
1857	## Proposal Cards
1858	
1859	Each proposal is a card in the panel, in the order given: a label at its top, "New story" in the theme's accent, or, for an addition, "Add to this story" where it targets the story the research or draft was started from, and "Add to" and the story's title otherwise, in the story's own mode's colour, so where it will go is always read before anything else on the card; its title, its mode pill, and its prompt beneath, clipped at four lines with "Read more"; and three buttons along its foot, "Accept", "Edit", and "Reject", reachable by Tab and labelled for a screen reader. Edit opens the card's title, prompt, mode, and target in place, the target a menu of "New story" and each story, to be changed before it is accepted; editing doesn't accept it. Reject removes the card, with a short "Undo" in its place for a few seconds.
1860	Accept records it in the plan straight away, saved as any change to the plan is: a new story goes into the Backlog, at its end, in its mode, marked "From agent" with a small sparkle beside its title until it is first opened, its spec citations kept with it, whether it was accepted on its own card or with "Accept all", and whether it came from drafting, research, or an Ask answer. Accepting never adds anything to Next sprint, so it never starts a sprint, however Start automatically is set; an accepted story reaches a sprint only once it is moved to Next sprint, as the sprint says; an addition is added to the named story as a new step at its end, as its steps say, its attachments with it, and the story is marked "Updated by agent" until it is next opened, the new step shown highlighted the first time it is; where the story no longer exists by then, the step isn't added, as the steps say, and the card stays, its target changed to "New story", to be accepted again. A story already sent can't be added to: its proposals offer only "New story". Each card, once decided, goes from the panel, and an accepted one leaves a one-line muted note in its place, "Added to Backlog" or "Added to <story>", with a link that opens the story where it is, in the Backlog or its section.
1861	Ask answers can propose the same way: a `suspense-story` block in an answer is shown as a proposal card, with the same Accept, Edit, and Reject, its accepting recording it in the plan as above, so a story can come out of a conversation without anything written silently.
1862	
1863	## Research
1864	
1865	The agent can be asked to research a topic before anything is planned or built: "Research", a button beside "Draft stories" on the Backlog's heading, and "Research" in an open story's menu, open a box labelled "What should be looked into?". Research runs as a read-only investigation, a Question run, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, which can read the project and the web and change nothing, given the research prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts), which asks for findings, not changes: what was found, where, with links to the files and lines it read, what it is unsure of, and what it would suggest, and it may end with proposals, as the proposals say. Its run is shown in the drafting panel as drafting's is, its live line of what it is reading, a Stop button, and its spinner.
1866	Its findings are a document of their own, "Research: <topic>", rendered as markdown with its links clickable, shown in a Findings list beneath the Backlog, newest first, each a row with its topic, when it ran, and its state, and opening in a body tab of its own to read whole. Findings started from a story are also listed in that story, beneath its steps. They are saved with the plan, in `.suspense/planning/research/`, a markdown file each, so they can be read again later, and can be deleted from their row's menu.
1867	
1868	## Paused
1869	
1870	Once research ends, however it ended, planning is paused. While it is paused nothing is implemented: Send sprint, the ribbon's Send Sprint, and the sprint's Ctrl+Shift+Enter are disabled, their tooltips saying planning is paused for review, and no proposal from the research is added to the plan by itself. Stories can still be written, edited, ordered, and moved, and proposals still accepted or rejected one by one, since those only change the plan.
1871	Nothing of the plan starts while it is paused, not only nothing new: a story of Current sprint still waiting in the queue, not yet started, is held where it is, as a queued prompt being edited is held, as the [QueueList](../prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list) says, its row reading "Held for review", muted, and its lane waits on it; a story already running when the pause began runs on to its end, since stopping it would leave its work half done, and the bar says how many are still running. A chain's next step, as a story's steps are sent, is held the same way. Once the pause ends, by Resume or Approve, what was held goes on in its order, as though nothing had stopped it.
1872	The pause is plain to see: a bar across the top of Planning, in the theme's warning colour, with a pause icon, reads "Paused for review", names the research it is waiting on, with a link that opens its findings, and holds two buttons, "Resume", which ends the pause, and "Approve and send sprint", which ends it and sends Next sprint at once. The Planning tab in the body shows a small pause icon beside its name, and the ribbon's Planning tab a warning dot, while it is paused. Pressing either button is the only way the pause ends; nothing the agent does, and no time passing, ends it. A second research while paused keeps the pause, naming the latest.
1873	The pause is saved with the plan, in `order.json`, with the research it waits on, as soon as it begins, so it is still paused, and still shown so, after the project is closed and opened again, the application restarted, or the window reloaded, until it is resumed or approved.
1874	
1875	## Keyboard
1876	
1877	Everything in Planning can be done from the keyboard. Tab moves through the section headings' buttons, the rows, and the open story's fields in order, and the focused one shows the theme's focus ring. In a list, Up and Down move between rows, Enter opens or closes the focused story, A accepts the focused proposal, E edits it, and R rejects it, and Alt+Up and Alt+Down move the focused story up or down, across sections as dragging does. Ctrl+N adds a story, Ctrl+Enter moves the focused story to Next sprint, or to the Backlog from it, Ctrl+Shift+Enter sends the sprint, and M opens the focused story's mode picker, whose options are picked with the arrow keys and Enter. Delete deletes the focused story after a confirmation. Escape closes what is open, a menu, a story, or the drafting or research panel, one at a time. Every button and control has a label a screen reader reads, as its visible text or, for an icon, its tooltip, and each shortcut is given in the tooltip of the control it stands for.
1878	Ctrl+Shift+D opens Draft stories, focusing its request box, where Enter starts the draft, as Ctrl+Enter also does, and Shift+Enter adds a new line; Ctrl+Shift+R opens Research, focusing its box, where Ctrl+Enter starts it; F6 moves focus between the column's regions, the pause bar, each section, an open panel, and back, so each is a single stop; within the pause bar, Tab reaches Resume and Approve and send sprint; within an open story, Tab reaches its steps, its Add step, and its Spec citations, each citation opening on Enter; and within Findings, Enter opens the focused finding in its tab. The Start automatically switch is reached by Tab on Next sprint's heading and toggled with Space. Focus never lands on something hidden or disabled, and after an action it stays where it was or moves to what the action made, as the new story or the next proposal, never back to the top.
1879	# Body
1880	
1881	## How To Build
1882	
1883	A Body should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A Body should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.
1884	
1885	## Theme
1886	
1887	Drawn in the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.
1888	
1889	## Pitch
1890	
1891	The main window's body: the area to the right of the project sidebar, where the tasks sent to the harness, and the files opened in tabs beside them, are shown, and the chat input they are sent from.
1892	
1893	## Description
1894	
1895	Beneath the [Ribbon](../../ui/components/ribbon/index.md#ribbon), to the right of the [LeftSidebar](../../ui/components/left-sidebar/index.md#left-sidebar), which runs the full height beside it, and reaching the window's right edge. It is part of the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor).
1896	The [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) lives within the body, along its bottom: its left edge against the project sidebar, and above it, beneath the body's tab bar, the selected tab's contents: the message list, or an open file. While a task runs, the [RightSidebar](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar) runs the body's full height at its right, beside the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, and the chat input, and the chat input's right edge is against it: the chat input never runs beneath the right sidebar. While that sidebar isn't there, the chat input reaches the window's right edge.
1897	The body is flat and quiet: the selected tab's contents, the message list or an open file, sit on the theme's base surface, #444444 in dark mode, running edge to edge with no border, and the chat input along the bottom is set apart from them only by its own darker tab strip, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) says, with no line between them.
1898	
1899	## Sliding
1900	
1901	Whenever something slides out or back along one of the body's edges, as the [RightSidebar](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar) does, everything else in the body moves smoothly with it, frame by frame, rather than jumping once the slide is over: the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, the Ask conversation while it shows, and the chat input all keep their right edge against the sliding edge throughout, so they narrow or widen together, in step with it and with each other. None of them lags behind another, is left at its old width until the slide settles, or runs beneath what is sliding. Their contents are laid out anew at each width as it changes, text wrapping and rows reflowing as they go: the tab bar's tabs, the chat input's text and buttons, the message list's table, and an open file's editor. A slide that reverses partway moves them back from wherever it had reached.
1902	
1903	## Contents
1904	
1905	Everything that can be in the body:
1906	
1907	- a tab bar along its top, holding a Chat tab, a tab for each file open, and the Planning tab while it is open
1908	- the [Planning](../planning/index.md#planning), beneath the tab bar while its tab is selected
1909	- the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list), the chat history, shown beneath the tab bar while the Chat tab is selected
1910	- the hint shown in the message list's place before any task has been sent, or while no project is open, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor) and the [NoProjectState](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state) say
1911	- an [Editor](../editor/index.md#editor) for each open file, shown beneath the tab bar while its tab is selected
1912	- a task view for each task opened in a tab of its own, as its task tabs say, shown beneath the tab bar while its tab is selected
1913	- the [AskConversation](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation), in the Chat tab's place beneath the tab bar, while the chat input's Ask tab is selected
1914	- the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input), along the bottom beneath whichever tab is selected, and beneath the Ask conversation too
1915	- the [RightSidebar](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar), at the right of all of these, the tab bar and the chat input included, while a task runs or is queued, or it is opened by hand
1916	
1917	An [InsetPanel](../../ui/components/inset-panel/index.md#inset-panel) floats over the whole window, the body included, but is never part of it.
1918	
1919	## Ask Mode
1920	
1921	While the chat input's Ask tab is selected, the Ask conversation, as the [AskConversation](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation) says, takes the Chat tab's place in the body, filling all of it beneath the tab bar and above the chat input, as the message list fills it for every other mode: the body never splits, and nothing is shown beside the conversation. The Chat tab then reads "Ask" in Ask's colour. Selecting another mode's tab brings the message list back in its place, as it was left, and selecting Ask again brings the conversation back, scrolled where it was; the switch is at once, with nothing sliding. A file or task tab selected shows that file or task whatever mode is selected, and selecting Ask while one is shown selects the Chat tab, so the conversation is in view.
1922	
1923	## Tabs
1924	
1925	Along the top of the body runs a tab bar, in gpui-kit's default tab styling, across the width the message list takes: from the project sidebar to the right sidebar while a task runs, and to the window's right edge otherwise. Its first tab, Chat, shows the message list, and is always there: it can't be closed or moved. After it comes a tab for each open file and each task opened in a tab of its own, files and tasks together, in the order they were opened unless they have been dragged since, scrolling sideways once there are more than fit.
1926	Just one tab's contents show at a time, filling the space between the tab bar and the chat input. The chat input stays along the bottom whichever tab is selected, so a prompt can be written while a file shows. The body starts with Chat selected, and clicking a tab selects it.
1927	Every tab in the bar, Chat and each file's alike, is laid out the same plain way, with nothing extra around it: the bar's full height, 32 pixels, its contents centred up and down in it, 12 pixels of padding at its left, and 12 at its right, and no margin of its own above, below, or beside it, so one tab ends where the next begins, with only the tab styling's own line between them. Nothing is inset from the bar's top or bottom, and the first tab starts at the bar's left edge.
1928	A file's tab shows the file's name, then, while it has unsaved changes, a dot, and then a small close button, an icon button 16 pixels square, set close beside the name, 4 pixels from it or from the dot, with no more room between them however long or short the name is. Since the button has room of its own around its icon, a file tab's right padding is 6 pixels rather than 12, so the icon sits as far from the tab's right edge as the name does from its left; the tab is only as wide as its padding, name, dot, and close button need. Chat's spinner, while something runs, sits 6 pixels after its label, inside the same padding. Hovering a file's tab shows the file's path in the project as its tooltip.
1929	A file's tab can be dragged along the tab bar to reorder the files, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, a vertical line showing the gap between two tabs it will land in, and the tab dragged following the pointer as the file's name. Chat stays first: no gap before a file's first tab, between Chat and it, shows the indicator, and Chat itself can't be dragged. Dragging a tab selects it, as clicking it does, and the selection follows the tab to its new place; nothing else about its editor changes. A press on a tab's close button closes it rather than starting a drag. A file opened afterwards still gets its new tab just after the one selected.
1930	
1931	## Task Tabs
1932	
1933	The Chat tab shows only the task the harness is working on now, and those running beside it, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s header shows them, or, while none runs, the task that finished last, until the next is sent. It never shows any other task: a task opened from the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTab](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab) says, or from anywhere else that opens a task, opens in a tab of its own in the body's tab bar, as a file does: a task not open yet gets a new tab just after the one selected, and is selected; opening one that already has a tab selects that tab; and opening the task Chat is showing selects Chat instead.
1934	A task's tab is laid out as a file's is: a bar 2 pixels wide down its left in its mode's colour, its status, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, then its name, the first line of its prompt cut off with an ellipsis at 24 characters, then its close button. Hovering it shows its prompt's first lines and its mode as its tooltip. It can be dragged among the files' tabs, and closed as they are, closing it changing nothing about the task.
1935	Beneath it, the task shows as it would at the head of the Chat tab, on its own: its header, with its status, time, compiled prompt, and buttons, then its output table, then the files it changed, scrolled to its top the first time it is shown, and as it was left after. A task still running shows its output as it comes, its table locked to the bottom while scrolled there, as the latest task's is, and carries on in its tab whether or not the tab is selected. Its tab stays open once it finishes. Opening a task in a tab doesn't select it in the Chat tab or change what Chat shows, and Chat's running tasks are never opened in tabs of their own unless asked for, a running task opened from the Tasks tab selecting it in Chat's header instead. Each open project keeps its own task tabs, as its file tabs are kept, and none is reopened when the project is opened again.
1936	
1937	## Open File
1938	
1939	A file opened, from the [FileTree](../../ui/components/file-tree/index.md#file-tree) or anywhere else the [OpenFile](../open-file/index.md#open-file) says, shows in an [Editor](../editor/index.md#editor) in a tab of its own, as many files open at once as are opened. A file not open yet gets a new tab, just after the one selected, and is selected. Opening a file that already has a tab selects that tab instead, leaving its editor as it was, unsaved changes and all.
1940	Nothing slides: a file's tab is selected, and its editor shows, at once, and closing it takes it away at once too. Files never split the body among themselves; the file takes the tab bar's full width above the chat input.
1941	Closing a file's tab, with its close button or the editor's, closes the file, the editor first asking to discard any unsaved changes. Closing the selected tab selects the tab to its right, or, with none to its right, the one to its left, which is Chat once no file is left. Closing a tab that isn't selected leaves the selection as it is.
1942

This project is written in Piton, a declarative language for agent guidance.

- Source of truth: the `.pi` files under `./spec`. Compiled Markdown is derived output.
- Make lasting changes in the Piton source, then run `piton build`; never hand-edit generated artifacts.
- Compiled reference documents live under `.claude/reference`. Links between them are lazy: follow one when the work touches what it describes.
- Scoped guidance is written to `CLAUDE.md` files placed next to the code they describe.
- `piton check` validates the specbase; `piton reach` shows what the entrypoints can see; `piton slice file.pi#Anchor.property` prints just the spec one thing depends on.

# Piton Fluency

This is a working reference for Piton, the Belay framework bundled with it, the
project configuration, the package manager and the tooling. Read it before you
read or change a Piton specbase. It is generated from the specification in
`spec/` by the GenerateFluencyPrompt skill. Where the compiler behaves
differently from the spec, the text below says so, and section 16 lists every
known gap.

## 1. What Piton is, and why

Piton is a declarative, whitespace-structured language for writing agent
guidance: skills, agents, commands, scoped instructions and reference
documents. Its author calls it a "semi-natural programming language". Prose and
structure are both first-class. A value can be a paragraph of plain English or
a typed, inherited, composed data structure, and most files mix the two.

The founding thesis (`spec/scope/founding-thesis/`) explains the design:

- Every programming language is an abstraction over the layer beneath it. Once
  an abstraction is accepted, nobody cares how its compiled output is produced,
  as long as the output is good. Agentic development is the next step in that
  history. In this model the agent is the compiler.
- Humans are good at designing coherent systems, not at typing out the latest
  accepted abstraction. Piton keeps the describing, constraining and thinking,
  and hands the manual labour to the agent.
- Prompting an agent session by session produces results that live in one
  developer's memory and cannot be traced. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Markdown
  skills help, but pure prose decays. It is ambiguous, it gets duplicated, and
  it has no tools for reuse. Piton adds imports, inheritance, types and
  references to prose, while keeping prose for the things prose says best
  ("the button should be blue with contrasting text"). Plain prompting is fine
  for a small one-off tool. A sufficiently complex system needs a traceable
  artifact of the process itself, not just its output, and more so when
  several people work on it.
- The real problem is repetition. Much software work is the same patterns
  again (CRUD APIs, layouts, navigation bars, modal forms). Functions, classes
  and generics are ways of wrapping a problem once it becomes a pattern. The
  aim is to keep designing systems and stop typing the patterns: "I never
  wanted to write code itself; I wanted to create."
- The CNC analogy: G-code replaced the machinist's hand, and CAM then sat on
  top of G-code by combining design intent with the machinist's expertise. The
  CAM engineer never types G-code but is essential. CNC did not replace most of
  the machinist's skill, and two jobs (engineer, machinist) became three (plus
  the CAM engineer). The Piton author plays that role for agents.
- The stated goal is that you can paste the specification into an agentic
  coding tool and get a compiler for Piton and Belay back. This repository is
  that experiment. The specification in `spec/` is written in Piton, and the
  compiler in `crates/` is judged against it.

Core facts:

- **There is no runtime.** Piton compiles to data (JSON, YAML, Markdown)
  through **renderers**. Frameworks such as Belay add **adapters** on top of
  the renderers. There are no functions, no loops, and no conditionals except
  the ternary operator. Every value is immutable.
- **The `.pi` source is the source of truth.** Compiled Markdown under
  `.claude/reference`, `.claude/skills`, `CLAUDE.md` files and so on is derived
  output. Make lasting changes in the `.pi` files and rebuild. Never hand-edit
  generated artifacts.
- A **specbase** is a Piton project: a `piton.config.pi`, a source root
  (usually `spec/`), an entry file, and the frameworks and packages it uses.
- **Successful compilation shows that the guidance is well-formed. It does not
  show that an agent will behave correctly.** Artifact generation is
  predictable, but agent behaviour is probabilistic.

## 2. Files, whitespace, comments, keywords

- Source files use the `.pi` extension. A directory that contains an
  `index.pi` is a module (section 7.2).
- **Indentation defines structure**, as in Python. Tabs or any number of
  spaces are accepted, but one file must be consistent. The canonical style is
  4 spaces. `piton format` enforces it, and it cannot be configured.
- **Comments** are line-only and start with `//`. There are no block comments.
  **A comment has to be on its own line.** After code, `//` is just text, so
  `url: https://example.com // note` is the string
  `https://example.com // note`. The formatter adds one space after `//` when
  there is none and touches nothing else in the comment, so commented-out code
  keeps its spacing. To start a value with `//`, escape it:
  `\ // \ Just Text`.
- **Reserved words** have special meaning:

  ```
  anchor abstract export from import use as extends pass
  this self super
  true false null
  any simple complex
  string number boolean list dictionary
  ```

  You can't use them as your own keywords (`reserved-keyword`), but **you can
  use them as keys**. As keys they are just strings: `null: text`,
  `use: text` and `as: text` are ordinary properties.
- **Keywords** are all lowercase and may be kebab-case
  (`arithmetic-operator`). Users define their own with `as` (section 8.6).
- **`pass`** fills the body of an anchor that has no properties of its own. An
  anchor always needs something indented under it; `anchor X:` with nothing
  under it is `empty-anchor`.

  ```piton
  anchor Child extends Base:
      pass
  ```

## 3. Declarations and values

A file is a sequence of top-level declarations. Top-level names are variables
scoped to their file: they are global within the file and invisible outside it
unless exported.

```piton
myVariable: 42
export pi: 3.14

export anchor MyAnchor:
    description: This is my anchor
```

`key: value` assigns a value, and the space after the colon is required. The
value can sit on the same line or be indented on the lines below:

```piton
sameLine: Hello, World!
nextLine:
    Hello, World!
```

Both produce `"Hello, World!"`. The leading indentation belongs to the syntax,
not to the string.

**A property has to have a value.** A name with nothing after it and nothing
indented under it is a compiler error (`empty-value`). If you mean nothing,
write `null`. The one exception is a required property in an abstract anchor
(`title:: string`); anywhere else a constraint with no value is
`missing-value`.

### 3.1 Types

Piton is loosely typed, with optional constraints.

| Type | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `string` | Unicode text. Never quoted (section 3.3). |
| `number` | One numeric type, a 64-bit IEEE 754 float, with no int/float distinction. |
| `boolean` | Lowercase `true` and `false`. |
| `null` | Lowercase `null`. It is the only "nothing" value (there is no `undefined`), and `{null == null}` is `true`. |
| `list` | An ordered collection. Item types may be mixed unless a constraint says otherwise. |
| `dictionary` | Key/value pairs. Keys are strings, and value types may be mixed unless constrained. |
| anchor | The one user-defined type (section 8). |

- **Simple types** are string, number, boolean and null.
- **Complex types** are list, dictionary and anchor.
- A **reference** is its own type, produced by `@{}` (section 6.5). It points
  at an anchor or a property on one instead of copying it.

- **Inference.** An unconstrained variable or property can hold any type,
  inferred from how the value looks: `true` is a boolean but `true story` is
  a string; `42` and `-42` are numbers but `42 things` is a string; `A + B`
  and `This costs $5 + tax` are strings (no braces, no expression); `null` is
  null; `"false"` is a string; `${a + b}` is always a string.

Every built-in type is described by an anchor that uses the abstract `type`
keyword (`spec/scope/language/types/lib/Type.pi`). A `type` anchor provides a
`description` (simple or complex) and its `supportedOperators` (a list of
operators, or null). Using an operator a type does not list is a compiler
error, but the compiler applies the coercion (4.2) and inference rules before
it reports one:

| Type | Supported operators |
| --- | --- |
| number | arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
| string | concatenation `+`, `++`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
| boolean | logical `&& \|\| !`, `==`, `!=` |
| null | `==`, `!=` |
| list | merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
| dictionary | `.`, merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
| anchor | `.`, `==`, `!=` |
| reference | `==`, `!=` |

### 3.2 Numbers

```piton
myInt: 123
myFloat: 3.14
mySmallFloat: 0.14
myBigNumber: 1_200_000.00
negative: -5
```

- **A decimal needs its leading `0`.** `0.14` is a number; `.5` is not a number
  (unconstrained, it is the string `".5"`).
- `_` may separate digits for readability.
- **There is no exponent notation.** `1e3` is not a number (unconstrained, it
  is silently the string `"1e3"`, not an error).
- A negative number is written with a minus, like `-5`. A list item always has
  a space after its dash, so `-5` is a number and `- 5` is a list item.
- **The minus is only part of a number.** There's no minus in front of an
  expression: `{-price}` is an error. Write `{0 - price}`.
- Compiled numbers take their shortest form: `1_200_000.00` becomes `1200000`
  and `0.50` becomes `0.5`.

### 3.3 Strings and quotes

- Strings are not quoted. **Quotes are ordinary characters in a value**, so
  `greeting: "Hello"` is the string `"Hello"`, quotes and all, and
  `"false"` is a string with quotes in it, never a boolean.
- The one exception is inside an expression, where bare words are symbols, so
  string operands are written in double quotes: `{"Hello" + name}`. There the
  quotes are not part of the string.
- In a multi-line block, consecutive lines join with one space. **A blank line
  starts a new paragraph**, which compiles to a line break (`\n`). Several
  blank lines in a row still count as one.

  ```piton
  myString:
      This broken string is not considered
      a line break.

      While this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above.
  ```

  This compiles to
  `"This broken string is not considered a line break.\nWhile this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above."`.

- **Markdown in a string is plain text.** Piton has no link syntax, so
  `[the guide](./guide.md)` and `![A diagram](./diagram.png)` pass through
  exactly as written. Nothing resolves, rewrites or checks them, and they are
  never an error. The only links Piton makes are `@{}` references.

### 3.4 Escaping

Escaping works by wrapping. Put backslashes around the special characters,
with a space on each side. The spaces are part of the wrapper and are removed:
`\ {1 + 2 + 3} \` compiles to the literal `{1 + 2 + 3}`. It is the only way to
escape, and even a single character gets wrapped: `\ : \` gives `:`.

- **Stacking.** To escape backslashes themselves, use more of them. The
  closing wrapper must match the opening one, so anything inside can use fewer:
  `\\ \ {x} \ \\` compiles to `\ {x} \`.
- **Multi-line escape blocks.** A line holding only backslashes opens a block,
  and a line with the same number of backslashes closes it. Everything in
  between is kept exactly, line breaks and indentation included. The spec uses
  three backslashes (`\\\`) for these.
- **Code fences are ordinary text.** A ```` ``` ```` fence does not protect
  anything: expressions, comments, list items and keys inside it are still
  parsed. So put an escape block inside the fence, the way every example in the
  spec does:

  ````piton
  description:
      ```piton
      \\\
      anchor Example:
          value: {1 + 2}
      \\\
      ```
  ````

  This keeps the fence and the example exactly as written. Markdown tables
  need the same treatment, because otherwise their rows join into one line.

**Prose pitfalls.** Each of these silently changes the structure of a string
block:

- A line that starts `- ` makes a list item, and a line that starts `+ ` or
  `++ ` makes a composition line (section 5). A property declared `:: string`
  then fails. Escape the start: `\ - \ item`.
- A line shaped like `word: text` (`Similarly: ...`, `Inputs: none`, or a
  wrapped line that happens to start with `type:`) becomes a dictionary key,
  and the block turns into an implicit list. Escape the colon (`\ : \`) or
  rewrap the paragraph.
- Backticks do not protect anything. `` `{x}` `` is still an expression, and
  `` `a + b` `` in a table cell is text only because it has no braces.
- An expression in running text changes the value's shape when it evaluates
  to a list, dictionary or anchor (section 6.2).

Wrapping stops text being parsed as syntax, but it doesn't change the inferred
type: `\ false \` is still the boolean `false`. To get the string, write
`${false}`.

The wrapper is the only way to escape. A backslash that doesn't open a
wrapper (a backslash followed by a space) is just a backslash, so `\:` is the
two characters `\:`. Write `\ : \` to escape a colon.

### 3.5 Lists

```piton
markdownStyle:
    - One
    - List
    - Item

inlineStyle: [This, is, a, list, of, strings]

nestedMarkdownList:
    - Level 1
        - Level 2
            - Level 3
```

`nestedMarkdownList` is `[Level 1, [Level 2, [Level 3]]]`.

- **Items cannot be accessed by index.** By design there is no `myList[0]`.
  Piton describes things; it does not compute them, and lists exist to be
  merged and inherited.
- **A list item is never a key**, even with a colon at the end. `- Settings:`
  is just the string `"Settings:"`.
- **Anything indented under a list item is not part of that item.** It becomes
  the next item in the list, so a dictionary indented under an item is its own
  item, right after it:

  ```piton
  repos:
      - https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs
          tag: v1
      - https://github.com/piton-lang/other
  ```

  This compiles to
  `["https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs", {"tag": "v1"}, "https://github.com/piton-lang/other"]`.
  A dictionary that ends up as an item of an explicit list cannot be addressed.

### 3.6 Dictionaries

A dictionary has one syntax, which is indentation:

```piton
firstLevel:
    secondLevel:
        thirdLevel: This is a string
```

- Dot access works: `{firstLevel.secondLevel.thirdLevel}` gives
  `"This is a string"`.
- **Valid keys** contain Unicode letters, Unicode digits, `_` and `-`, and
  nothing else (no spaces, no dots). Keys are always strings, even when they
  look like something else, so `thisIsAKey`, `123`, `foo-bar`, `false` and
  `null` are valid keys, while `This is a key` and `a.b` are not.
- **A hyphen inside a name is part of the name.** `{config.foo-bar}` reads the
  key `foo-bar`. For subtraction, put spaces around the minus: `{a - b}`.
- A list indented under a key is that key's value. If the key also has
  something above the list, like text or another dictionary, the value becomes
  an implicit list (3.7) and the list goes in as one item:

  ```piton
  plain:
      - x
      - y
  mixed:
      text
      - x
      - y
  ```

  `plain` is `["x", "y"]`; `mixed` is `["text", ["x", "y"]]`.

### 3.7 Implicit lists

A block that mixes prose, list items and keys becomes an **implicit list**
that keeps the source order:

```piton
combined:
    This is a string

    - This
    - Is
    - A
    - List

    nestedDictionary:
        deeplyNestedDictionary: This is a string
```

This compiles to
`["This is a string", ["This", "Is", "A", "List"], {"nestedDictionary": {"deeplyNestedDictionary": "This is a string"}}]`.

- **Keys declared directly in the mixed block stay addressable.**
  `{combined.nestedDictionary.deeplyNestedDictionary}` still resolves.
- The prose and list elements cannot be addressed, because there is no list
  access.
- An expression in running text that gives a list, dictionary or anchor also
  makes an implicit list (section 6.2).

## 4. Variables and type constraints

- A variable is declared by naming it at the top level of a file:
  `myVariable: 42`.
- The file is its scope. `export` makes it visible to other files.
- **Inside an expression, a plain name always means a variable from the file
  (or something imported), even inside an anchor.** To reach a property on the
  anchor you are in, use `this` or `self`:

  ```piton
  x: top-level

  anchor Card:
      x: card
      fromFile: {x}
      fromCard: {this.x}
  ```

  `Card.fromFile` is `"top-level"` and `Card.fromCard` is `"card"`.
- Everything is immutable. There is no compile-time mutability.

### 4.1 Constraint syntax

A constraint is written `name:: type: value`. **The whitespace after `::` and
after `:` is mandatory**, so `myVariable::number:42` is an error
(`constraint-spacing`), in blocks as well as at the top level.

```piton
count:: number: 42
tags:: string[]: [foo, bar, baz]
config:: dictionary:
    a:: number: 1
    b:: string: foo
a:: complex: [1, 2, 3]
c:: simple: 1
g:: any: 1
h:: any:
    - String
    - [1, 2, 3]
```

- `simple` accepts string, number, boolean or null. `complex` accepts list,
  dictionary or anchor. `any` accepts anything.
- `T[]` is a list of `T`, for any type, including anchor types (`Foo[]`).
- `extends Foo[]` (or `extends Foo`) accepts anything that inherits from the
  anchor `Foo` (section 8.4). You can use it anywhere, but it is most at home
  in abstracts. The spec also uses it on exported lists:
  `export ARITHMETIC_OPERATORS:: extends ArithmeticOperator[]: ...`.
- An anchor-typed constraint (`f:: Foo: {Foo}`) is satisfied by the anchor or a
  copy of it (section 6.1).
- A file that names an abstract as a type must import it with
  `from ./Foo import Foo`. `use` alone is not enough (section 7.3).

### 4.2 Multiple constraints and coercion

Coercion is intentionally limited. With several constraints, they are tried
**left to right** and the first type the value can validly represent wins.

```piton
first:: number:: string: 42
second:: string:: number: 42
written:: string: 1.0
evaluated:: string: {1.0}
quoted:: boolean:: number:: string: "false"
```

- `first` is the number `42`; `second` is the string `"42"`.
- **A literal keeps its text when coerced to a string.** `written` is
  `"1.0"`. An expression is evaluated first and its result is coerced, so
  `evaluated` is `"1"`.
- `quoted` is the string `"false"`, quotes and all, because quotes are
  ordinary characters and `"false"` is not a boolean.
- **Booleans and null are never coerced**, to strings or anything else. `flag:: string: false`
  is a compiler error (`type-mismatch`), not the string `"false"`. If you want
  the string, write `${false}`.
- Lists, dictionaries and anchors are never coerced into unrelated types.
- If no constraint accepts the value, compilation fails with `type-mismatch`.
- These rules are about constraints. Operators such as `+` have their own
  rules (section 6.4).

### 4.3 Required and optional properties

In an abstract anchor:

```piton
abstract anchor Card:
    title:: string
    subtitle:: string:: null
    footer:: string:: null: null

anchor MyCard extends Card:
    title: Hello
    subtitle: null
```

- A constraint with no value is **required**. Anything that extends the anchor
